DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme

The report collects useful data and makes a sensible, low-cost proposal. However, it has one arithmetic error that changes a headline claim, and its central finding (that reminders raise uptake by 13 points) is not supported by the comparison it relies on. Both need fixing before this goes to the Health and Wellbeing Board.

## 1. Overall uptake is 62.4%, not 66.0%

From Table 1: 13,772 vaccinated ÷ 22,080 eligible = **62.4%**.

This affects the report in three places:
- **Section 3:** Eastvale did **not** meet the 65% national ambition. It fell about 2.6 points short. The statement that it was exceeded "for the first time" must be removed or corrected.
- **Table 1:** The "All schools" uptake figure is wrong.
- **Summary and recommendation:** The gap to the 70% target is about 7.6 points, not 4.

The other table figures check out:

| Group | Consent return | Uptake | Vaccinated among consented |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reminder | 75.0% | 70.0% | 93.3% |
| Non-reminder | 61.5% | 57.0% | 92.7% |
| All | 67.1% | 62.4% | 93.0% |

The non-reminder consent figure (61.5%) would usually be shown as 62% or 61.5% rather than 61%. This is minor.

## 2. The 13-point gap does not show that reminders caused 13 points of uptake

This is the most important problem. Schools chose whether to opt in, and the report itself shows that the two groups differ in ways that strongly affect uptake:

- **School nurses:** 76% of reminder schools have a full-time nurse (29 of 38), compared with 20% of non-reminder schools (11 of 54).
- **Affluence and geography:** Reminder schools are mostly in the more affluent west. Non-reminder schools include the eastern wards, which have more families who don't speak English at home and higher household mobility.
- **Self-selection:** Schools that chose to opt in may also be more engaged with the programme in general.

Any of these factors could explain much or all of the 13-point gap. The statements "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points" (Section 3) and "Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points" (Section 6) are causal claims the data can't support. The difference should be described as an association, with the confounding stated explicitly.

The report's own data could give a better estimate:
- **Before-and-after comparison:** Compare each school's change in uptake from 2024-25 to 2025-26, reminder schools against non-reminder schools (a difference-in-differences). This removes stable differences between schools.
- **Stratification:** Compare reminder and non-reminder schools *within* nurse and non-nurse groups, and within east and west.
- **Consent timing:** Use portal data to check whether consents rose after each text was sent.

## 3. The projected effect in non-reminder schools is likely overstated even if reminders work

Section 4 contains evidence that undermines the Section 6 projection:

- **Missing mobile numbers:** Only 61% of families in non-reminder schools have a valid mobile number on record, against 93% in reminder schools. Even if reminders work equally well, they can reach only about two-thirds as many families. That alone would shrink a 13-point effect to roughly 8–9 points before any other adjustment.
- **Language:** The lowest-uptake schools have more families who speak another language at home. An English-language text linking to an English-language portal may be less effective there.
- **Incomplete forms:** Reminders encourage families to return forms. They do nothing about forms returned incomplete, which is a separate barrier in these schools.
- **A ceiling already reached:** Some non-reminder schools already reach 79%. The claim of "bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" assumes a uniform effect, but the barriers are concentrated in the east.

The claim that reminders would raise non-reminder schools "from 57% to around 70%" should be replaced with a range, and the low-reach issue should be acknowledged.

## 4. Unsupported comparative claims

- **"More than any other intervention we have tried" (Section 3):** No other intervention is evaluated in the report. The only comparison offered is mop-up sessions (3–6 points), and that figure comes from staff reports, not measured data. Either support this claim or remove it.
- **"By far the cheapest route" (Section 6):** This may well be true per message. However, cost per *extra child vaccinated* depends on the real effect size, which is uncertain (see section 2 above). Mop-up sessions are only mentioned, not costed, so the comparison isn't made.

## 5. Cost section

The arithmetic is correct:
- Non-reminder schools: 4,990 × 3 × £0.08 = £1,198
- Existing reminder schools: 2,280 × 3 × £0.08 = £547
- First year including the £2,500 set-up charge: about £4,245, which is under £5,000

Two small points:
- The 4,990 figure counts **pupils** without consent, not **families**. Siblings would reduce the number of families. Missing mobile numbers would reduce real spending further, so the estimate is conservative. Note this, but it isn't a problem.
- The low cost is a real strength. It means the proposal can be justified even if the true effect is modest. The report would be more persuasive if it argued on that basis than if it relied on an overstated 13-point effect.

## 6. Suggested changes to the recommendation

- **Keep the recommendation to extend reminders**, since the cost is low and the risk is small. Base it on a modest, realistic expected effect rather than 13 points.
- **Add an action to improve mobile-number coverage** in eastern schools. Without this, reminders can't reach a large share of the target families.
- **Consider translated messages**, or a portal that supports the main community languages.
- **Phase the rollout in a way that allows real evaluation.** For example, introduce reminders across non-reminder schools in a randomised or staggered order. This would give the Board a sound estimate of the effect for 2027-28 decisions.
- **Address the other barriers directly:** set out options for mop-up sessions and for help completing consent forms, since these affect the lowest-uptake schools.
- **Make the end-of-season report specific:** report uptake by school alongside prior-year baselines, nurse status and ward, not just raw uptake.

## Minor points

- The Summary should state the corrected overall uptake and avoid the causal "13 points" framing.
- Section 4: give the uptake range for reminder schools too, so the two groups can be compared.
- State how many of the 14 mop-up schools were reminder schools, because this could also affect the comparison.
